description: Sabotages for the probation tier's results -- probation-common.ps1, run-tier.ps1, publish-probation-results.ps1 and report-probation.ps1 -- judged by test-probation.ps1. Run with tools/run-sabotage.ps1 -Manifest tools/sabotage-probation.json -CargoCommand tools/sabotage-probation-runner.cmd; see tools/README-sabotage.md.

sabotages.name: a failure does not end the run of passes
sabotages.why: The run of passes is what promotion is decided on. A failure that leaves it standing would show a test that failed last night as having passed every night.

sabotages.name: a pass is not counted as a pass
sabotages.why: The record gives passes beside runs, and a candidate is judged on them.

sabotages.name: a run already applied is applied again
sabotages.why: A publisher that retries from a fresh fetch applies the run to what it fetched, which may already hold it. Counted twice, a test is a run nearer promotion than it has earned.

sabotages.name: the latest run does not move on
sabotages.why: The report knows a test was not in the latest run by its last run being another. A latest run that never moves leaves a promoted or deleted test reading as current.

sabotages.name: a candidate needs one pass more than the threshold
sabotages.why: The threshold is the passes in a row that make a candidate, so a test at it is one.

sabotages.name: a test whose last run failed is not called failing
sabotages.why: A test that has passed four in a row and failed the fifth is not a candidate, and the report says what it is.

sabotages.name: a test the latest run did not report is called current
sabotages.why: A test promoted to long_haul stops being reported. Its streak stands in the record, and without this it would be listed as a candidate for what it no longer is.

sabotages.name: a threshold of zero is accepted
sabotages.why: Every test has passed zero runs in a row, so a threshold of zero makes every test a candidate.

sabotages.name: a test that started and never reported is counted as a pass
sabotages.why: A test that aborts its process is the case probation exists for. Counted as a pass, or as nothing, it would be promoted.

sabotages.name: a test left pending by one executable is carried into the next
sabotages.why: Its name would then be recorded under the next executable's target, which is a different test.

sabotages.name: a test left pending at the end of the capture is dropped
sabotages.why: The last executable is the one a crash is most likely to end the capture in.
find: & $closeTarget # the end of the capture closes the last executable
replace: $null = 0 # the end of the capture closes the last executable

sabotages.name: a test is keyed by its file name and not its source path
sabotages.why: Two crates both have a src/lib.rs and a tests/integration.rs. Keyed by the leaf, their tests are one test.

sabotages.name: an executable that is not a test build is a test executable
sabotages.why: A library or binary build names an executable that is not a test harness, and a header naming one would be given a target that has no tests.

sabotages.name: a record of another version is read as this one
sabotages.why: A layout this does not know, read as this one, publishes over it with a record the other reader cannot read.

sabotages.name: the keys are sorted by the host's culture
sabotages.why: A record is compared as text, so two hosts must write the same bytes. Culture order puts a before B and ordinal does not.

sabotages.name: a time read as a DateTime is written in the host's own format
sabotages.why: PowerShell 7 reads an ISO 8601 string out of JSON as a DateTime, and written back it would come out as 01/01/2026 00:00:00 and differ from what the branch holds, so every publish would commit.

sabotages.name: the push is forced
sabotages.why: A rejected push means another publisher moved the branch since the fetch. Forcing it past that overwrites the run they published.

sabotages.name: an unreachable remote is read as an absent branch
sabotages.why: `ls-remote --exit-code` exits 2 for no matching ref and 128 for a remote it could not ask. A publisher that took the second for the first would write a root commit over history it could not see.

sabotages.name: the branch is asked for by its bare name
sabotages.why: ls-remote matches a pattern against the tail of each ref, so the bare name also finds refs/heads/other/probation-results.

sabotages.name: a run the branch already holds is published again
sabotages.why: Publishing it again would add a commit that changes nothing, on every retry and every re-publish.

sabotages.name: a run that selected nothing creates the branch
sabotages.why: The first run, before any test is on probation, would create a branch holding an empty record.

sabotages.name: a commit is made without its parent
sabotages.why: A root commit over a branch the remote already has is not a fast-forward, and is refused every time.

sabotages.name: a branch that could not be asked about is published over anyway
sabotages.why: The error is the only thing that says the remote was unreachable and not empty.

sabotages.name: missing outcomes exit zero
sabotages.why: A publisher that was not given what it publishes must not look like one that published.
find: Write-Host "No outcomes to publish at $Outcomes."; exit 2
replace: Write-Host "No outcomes to publish at $Outcomes."; exit 0

sabotages.name: a remote that cannot be asked exits zero
sabotages.why: A report of nothing is not a report of an empty record.

sabotages.name: the report is not appended to the step summary
sabotages.why: The summary is where the result of a run is read.

sabotages.name: libtest is not asked for its JSON output
sabotages.why: The unstable format is what carries each test's outcome, and it is asked for with RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP, which libtest honours whatever the value is set to, so the entry removes the variable. Without it the run is text, and nothing is read from it.

sabotages.name: the step does not exit with cargo's code
sabotages.why: A failing probation test fails its step; that is how it is seen.

sabotages.name: ignored tests are not asked for
sabotages.why: A tier's tests are ignored, so a run that does not pass --ignored runs none of them.

sabotages.name: a build that failed exits zero
sabotages.why: A run over tests that did not build is not a run that found nothing wrong.

sabotages.name: the record's tests are told apart without regard to case
sabotages.why: A Rust test name is case-sensitive and two can differ only by case. Compared without regard to it, they are one test in the record, and one test's failures are another's passes. `[ordered]@{}` and PowerShell's own object properties both compare this way, which is how the record came to be an ordinal dictionary and a list.

sabotages.name: a tier runs its tests in parallel
sabotages.why: A tier's tests are the ones whose scale or timing is the point, so each runs alone. Run in parallel they load one another, and the flush-barrier stress instruments once collided on a temp file that way; a result taken under that load would be recorded against the test.

sabotages.name: cargo is not told to use no colour
sabotages.why: The executable headers are read as plain text. A host that sets CARGO_TERM_COLOR=always has cargo wrap them in escape codes, and then no executable is recognised and the run cannot be read.

sabotages.name: the run's cargo arguments are joined without quoting
sabotages.why: The build took each argument whole, as an array; the batch file the run goes through must pass each of them whole as well, and a path with a space in it comes apart if it is only joined.

sabotages.name: a percent sign in an argument is left for the batch file to expand
sabotages.why: In a batch file %NAME% is replaced by the variable's value, so a directory that has one in its name reaches cargo as a different directory unless the percent signs are doubled.

sabotages.name: an argument cmd cannot carry is not refused
sabotages.why: A double quote has no spelling that cmd and the C runtime read the same way, so the argument is refused up front and not passed half understood.

sabotages.name: lines of the capture that are not events are passed over
sabotages.why: A line that could not be read is a result that may have been lost, and the record treats a test a run does not report as one that was not run. Writing outcomes anyway would record a partial run as the whole one.

sabotages.name: a run is applied once only if it is the latest
sabotages.why: A run replayed after a later one, a re-run of the keeping job over an older artifact, would be counted again and its results put over the later run's, hiding a failure.

sabotages.name: the publisher compares only the latest run
sabotages.why: The branch is asked whether it holds the run, and holding it means having applied it, whichever run came after.

sabotages.name: the applied runs are not written to the record
sabotages.why: A list that is not kept is forgotten by the next publisher, which reads the record from the branch.

sabotages.name: a latest run is not counted as applied when the record has no list
sabotages.why: A record written before the list existed names its latest run, and that run has been applied.

sabotages.name: an executable is read from the last parenthesis of its header
sabotages.why: The directory above an executable can have parentheses in it (Program Files (x86)); the file name cannot.

sabotages.name: the batch file is written to the output directory
sabotages.why: The caller chooses the output directory, and cmd reads a %NAME% in the path of a batch file it is started with as a variable.

sabotages.name: a percent sign in the capture path is left for the batch file to expand
sabotages.why: In a batch file a redirect to a path with %NAME% in it goes to wherever the variable's value names.

sabotages.name: CONTROL: the explanation on the branch is reworded
sabotages.why: The manifest checking itself. This changes what a reader of the branch sees and nothing a test claims, so it MUST survive -- if it comes back caught, the suite is matching on incidental wording rather than behaviour, and its other results are worth less than they look.
